options.value: Killer of Men follows Mace, an enslaved man forced into mandingo fights. After killing an opponent, he stumbles upon the burial of the man he killed, igniting a reckoning with guilt, faith, and the violence shaping his life and identity.
Mace, an enslaved man forced to kill in brutal underground fights, must confront his faith, his heritage, and his humanity when he discovers an unexpected connection to his latest opponent.

KILLER OF MEN -- In 1834 South Carolina, an enslaved man is forced to fight to the death for spectacle, and survival. But every victory means killing one of his own. When he stumbles upon his opponent's burial rites, he finds the ceremony being held in the ancient faith of their shared ancestors, who he must now face to decide whether he will kill again.

history.by: Luke, in chat — two candidate synopses

options.value: KILLER OF MEN is a powerful and intense exploration of a man, Mace, who is trapped in the brutal reality of slavery and forced combat. It combines elements of historical fiction with spiritual and psychological themes, particularly focusing on Mace's internal struggle and his connection to his African roots and gods, like Ogun, the god of war in Yoruba religion.

Growing up, I was always one of the youngest in my year, but my height made me one of the tallest in the class. I was often one of the biggest in the room. As I got older, I started noticing how my mere presence was often seen as either a point of praise or persecution. My physicality, tied so closely to my skin, made me seem more menacing, more dangerous than the other boys—even those bigger and stronger than I was. It’s never anything overt, but small, incessant microaggressions. Death by a 1000 needles. It’s a plight that’s shaped me throughout my life, leaving me hyper-aware of myself in spaces. This experience, this reality, is tied to the plight of the Black man in America.

The concept of Mandingo fighting has always fascinated me. It’s a strange, bastardized idea in media and literature. To me, it represents many things: the commercialization of sports and entertainment, the myth of Black-on-Black crime, the portrayal of savagery in history, and the media. It’s always been used to showcase the “Black brute,” but it has never been shown subjectively from the perspective of those involved. What are their lives like? What do they hold dear? What keeps a man going when he’s put in a situation like that?
Setting this film in slavery times, rather than in the present day or during the 1960s, allows me to examine the deep-rooted history of this aggression. Visually, I want the fight scenes to reflect the physical sports Black men often participate in—body slams, boxing, football tackles—to show history repeating itself through various forms of expression.
By setting the story in the 1800s, I also had the chance to explore my heritage. With slavery still in full force and new enslaved people being brought in from Africa, I can examine the past in different ways.
I want to delve into the spirituality of the enslaved at the time, capturing the mix of cultures, beliefs, and religions that slowly formed what we now know as Black culture.

Killer of Men is an expression of pain—absolute brutality and suffering. But it’s also a story of resilience, culture, and spirituality. This story has kept me awake at night, terrified of what I’m putting on the screen.
Killer of Men has been a grueling process—one that’s forced me to question a lot of myself as a man and as a storyteller. This is my Oriki, my folktale, my poem. I won’t shy away from telling difficult stories or giving a voice to the voiceless. I will honor my ancestors and my culture in everything I do.

fields.label: Statement
fields.value:
Growing up, I was always one of the youngest in my year, but my height made me one of the tallest in the class. I was often one of the biggest in the room. As I got older, I started noticing how my mere presence was often seen as either a point of praise or persecution. My physicality, tied so closely to my skin, made me seem more menacing, more dangerous than the other boys—even those bigger and stronger than I was. It’s never anything overt, but small, incessant microaggressions. Death by a 1000 needles. It’s a plight that’s shaped me throughout my life, leaving me hyper-aware of myself in spaces. This experience, this reality, is tied to the plight of the Black man in America.

The concept of Mandingo fighting has always fascinated me. It’s a strange, bastardized idea in media and literature. To me, it represents many things: the commercialization of sports and entertainment, the myth of Black-on-Black crime, the portrayal of savagery in history, and the media. It’s always been used to showcase the “Black brute,” but it has never been shown subjectively from the perspective of those involved. What are their lives like? What do they hold dear? What keeps a man going when he’s put in a situation like that?
Setting this film in slavery times, rather than in the present day or during the 1960s, allows me to examine the deep-rooted history of this aggression. Visually, I want the fight scenes to reflect the physical sports Black men often participate in—body slams, boxing, football tackles—to show history repeating itself through various forms of expression.
By setting the story in the 1800s, I also had the chance to explore my heritage. With slavery still in full force and new enslaved people being brought in from Africa, I can examine the past in different ways.
I want to delve into the spirituality of the enslaved at the time, capturing the mix of cultures, beliefs, and religions that slowly formed what we now know as Black culture.

Killer of Men is an expression of pain—absolute brutality and suffering. But it’s also a story of resilience, culture, and spirituality. This story has kept me awake at night, terrified of what I’m putting on the screen.
Killer of Men has been a grueling process—one that’s forced me to question a lot of myself as a man and as a storyteller. This is my Oriki, my folktale, my poem. I won’t shy away from telling difficult stories or giving a voice to the voiceless. I will honor my ancestors and my culture in everything I do.

Growing up, I was always one of the youngest in my year, but my height made me one of the tallest in the class, and often the biggest in the room. As I got older, I started noticing how my mere presence was read as either a point of praise or persecution. My physicality, tied so closely to my skin, made me seem more menacing, more dangerous than the other boys, even those bigger and stronger than I was. It's never anything overt, but small, incessant microaggressions. Death by a million needles. These interactions have shaped me throughout my life, leaving me hyper-aware of myself in spaces, even in this country I call home. This experience, this reality, is the plight of all Black men in America.

Killer of Men is an expression of pain: absolute brutality and suffering. But it's also a story of resilience, culture, and spirituality. This story has kept me awake at night, terrified of what I'm putting on the screen.

The concept of Mandingo fighting has always fascinated me. It's a strange, bastardized idea in media and literature. To me, it represents many things: the commercialization of sports and entertainment, the myth of Black-on-Black crime, the portrayal of savagery in history and in the media. It has always been used to showcase the animalistic Black brute. Rarely, if ever, has an audience been invited into the subjective perspective of the fighters themselves. What are their lives like? What do they hold dear? What keeps a man going when he's put in a situation like that?

Setting this film during the period of American slavery, rather than in the present day or during the 1960s, allows me to examine the deep-seated historical roots of this aggression. Visually, I wanted the fight scenes to reflect the physical sports Black men often participate in, body slams, boxing, football tackles, to illustrate history repeating itself through various forms of expression. Early 1800s America also gave me the chance to explore my own heritage. With American chattel slavery at its peak and the transatlantic trade still bringing enslaved people ashore every year, we can examine themes we still recognize today as they were in the darkest hour of African Americans.

A critical piece of this film is the spirituality of the enslaved at the time: their mix of cultures, beliefs and religions that slowly formed what we now recognize as Black culture. Killer of Men has been a grueling process, one that's forced me to question a lot of myself as a man and as a storyteller. This is my Oriki, my folktale, my poem. I won't shy away from telling difficult stories or giving a voice to the voiceless. I will honor my ancestors and my culture in everything I do.

fields.label: Director bio — Jordan Betine
fields.value: Jordan Betine is a Nigerian-American filmmaker raised between Lagos, Nigeria, and Ashburn, Virginia. He earned his undergraduate degree in film from Howard University. Jordan studied Directing at the American Film Institute, where he directed six short films across genres, including historical drama, social realism, and surrealist comedy. His thesis film, "Killer of Men," is a historical drama set in 1830s South Carolina about an enslaved man who is forced into underground prizefighting. His work explores power, identity, and the African diaspora.

fields.label: Producer bio
fields.value: Ruoxiao Li is a storyteller from China. A graduate of the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, she is currently pursuing a degree in Producing at the American Film Institute. She is mentored by Lianne Halfon, whose notable works include Juno and Ghost World.

fields.label: Cinematographer bio — Luke Scroggins
fields.value: Luke Scroggins studied theater under David Connelly at the North East School of the Arts in his home town of San Antonio and continued at Otterbein University School of Theatre, earning a BFA in Acting. Television credits include SWITCHED AT BIRTH, GENERAL HOSPITAL and DAYS OF OUR LIVES. After a period coordinating and editing for fashion clients, Scroggins joined the Dark Side and began working in camera. Recently he has moved into the narrative space as Utility on the independent feature FRESH KILLS and the limited series RZR. He made his cinematographer debut on the short films COSMIC BEACH and L'DIRECTOR

fields.label: Production designer bio
fields.value: Rajarajeshwari "RJ" Ragampudi, is a recent graduate with a bachelor's degree in Architecture from India. She is recognized in her university for her undergraduate thesis, an in-depth research-based design project through the study of the films of the Indian film director, Satyajit Ray. Her experience as an Architect has helped her gain practical knowledge in spatial design, construction and project management. Along with this, she is also skilled in creative visualization with a stark interest in Film, enabling her to pursue an MFA degree in Production Design. She strives to design sets that are not only authentic to the setting but deeply character-driven, enhancing and punctuating key moments in the story.

fields.label: AFI boilerplate and fellows
fields.value:
AFI FELLOWS, as the sheet lists them
Ruoxiao Li, AFI Producing Fellow
Rajarajeshwari Ragampudi, AFI Production Design Fellow
Luke Scroggins, AFI Cinematography Fellow
Jordan Uwhubetine, AFI Directing Fellow
You Wu, AFI Editing Fellow

BOILERPLATE, verbatim
"The characters and events depicted in this motion picture are fictitious. Any similarity to actual
persons, living or dead, is purely coincidental."

"This motion picture is the property of the American Film Institute and is protected under the copyright
laws of the United States and other countries. Unauthorized duplication, distribution or exhibition may
result in civil liability and criminal prosecution."

"Produced at the AFI Conservatory in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the Master of Fine Arts
Degree or Certificate of Completion."

"Edited on Avid Media Composer"

© copyright MMXXV
American Film Institute
[AFI Conservatory logo]

THE DIRECTOR'S NAME DOES NOT MATCH. The fellows list reads "Jordan Uwhubetine"; the poster, the billing
block and every other credit read "Jordan Betine". It may be his legal name against his professional one.
Do not print either until Jordan says which. The sheet also spells the discipline "Directring", plainly a
typo for Directing, corrected above.

THE COPYRIGHT YEAR IS MMXXV, 2025, while 3.5 records completion as 2026. One of the two is wrong, or the
copyright is dated to the year of creation rather than completion. Worth settling before submission,
because festivals read both.

STILL OPEN ON THIS PAGE: vendor logos and the Green Seal are placeholders; the camera-equipment courtesy
line is unresolved, marked "delete if from AFI"; and the animal-welfare line carries the question "Did you
work with the Humane Society?" — the crawl bills a snake wrangler, so an animal was on set and the
American Humane wording needs checking.
